issues.legal_issue: A High Court should not quash a revisional order when the authority exercised its discretion on relevant grounds and the order contains no apparent error of law.
material_facts: An eviction order and its confirmation were reversed by the State Government in revision.
The tenant had operated a cinema in the premises for many years and had obtained a cinema licence from the District Magistrate.
The State Government considered the tenant’s long occupation and the circumstances surrounding the licence relevant to whether eviction was inexpedient.
The Supreme Court found no apparent error of law in the State Government’s order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the State Government’s revisional order; the order should stand.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court could not interfere merely because it might assess the circumstances differently; the State Government’s discretionary decision under sections 7-A and 7-F of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, was not vitiated where its reasons were relevant and there was no error of law apparent on the face of the record.

predicates.writ_review_of_revisional_order: The proceeding challenges an administrative authority’s revisional order through a writ petition.
predicates.relevant_discretionary_factors_considere: The revisional authority considered circumstances relevant to whether eviction should be ordered, including the occupant’s long use of the premises and the circumstances of the licence.
predicates.no_apparent_error_of_law: The revisional order contains no error of law apparent on the face of the record.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding challenges a revisional order, the order should stand if the authority considered relevant discretionary factors and the order contains no apparent error of law.

issues.legal_issue: A person who occupies accommodation as a tenant remains within the protection against eviction suits even without an allotment order.
material_facts: The tenant occupied the premises under a lease made without an allotment order.
The tenant paid rent to the original owner and later to the purchasers of the premises.
The purchasers brought a civil suit to recover possession without first obtaining the District Magistrate’s permission.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was a tenant protected by the restriction on eviction suits, and the suit brought without the required permission was not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(g) and 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, together with the scheme of the Act, include a person from whom rent is payable even if the person occupies without an allotment order. The Court approved Udho Dass v. Prem Prakash, (1963) A.L.J. 406, on the validity between the parties of a lease made without the required allotment. Section 3(1) prohibits an eviction suit against a tenant without the District Magistrate’s permission.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and rent_payable_by_occupant and no_allotment_order and required_permission_not_obtained

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brings a civil proceeding to evict an occupant from accommodation.
predicates.rent_payable_by_occupant: The occupant pays rent, or would owe rent under an express or implied agreement, for the accommodation.
predicates.no_allotment_order: The occupant’s possession was not based on an allotment order from the responsible authority.
predicates.required_permission_not_obtained: The landlord brings the eviction suit without first obtaining the permission required from the responsible authority.

issues.definition: A civil eviction suit is not maintainable when the occupant owes rent for the accommodation, has no allotment order, and the landlord has not obtained the required permission.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot waive by contract a statutory restriction on eviction suits that is founded on public policy.
material_facts: The lease stated that neither party would claim the benefit of the rent-control legislation and that its provisions would not apply to the lease.
The landlord brought an eviction suit without obtaining the permission required by the legislation.
The Court found that the restriction protected tenants, a weaker section, and served the wider community by limiting eviction suits without reasonable grounds.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not waive the protection, and the lease clause did not make the suit maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, is prohibitive and embodies public policy by protecting tenants and limiting eviction suits without reasonable grounds. Under section 23 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement whose object defeats a legal provision is void. The Court considered Lachoo Mal v. Radhey Shyam, [1971] 3 S.C.R. 693, and Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya Das, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 406, and held that the tenant could not waive this protection.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and statutory_permission_required and permission_not_obtained and contract_purports_to_waive_tenant_protection and protection_serves_public_policy

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: A landlord brings a civil proceeding to evict an occupant from accommodation.
predicates.statutory_permission_required: The governing law requires the landlord to obtain permission from a responsible authority before bringing the eviction suit.
predicates.permission_not_obtained: The landlord brings the eviction suit without obtaining that required permission.
predicates.contract_purports_to_waive_tenant_protec: The lease states that the tenant will not claim the statutory protection against eviction.
predicates.protection_serves_public_policy: The protection is intended to shield a weaker class from unjustified eviction proceedings and serves the interests of the community.

issues.definition: A contractual waiver is ineffective where a civil eviction suit requires prior permission, that permission was not obtained, the contract purports to surrender the tenant’s protection, and the protection serves public policy.
